description:
One of the most colourful geothermal parks in the world, about 30 minutes south of Rotorua. Well formed walking trails pass the Champagne Pool and the Artist's Palette, and the Lady Knox Geyser erupts on a set daily schedule. Paid entry.

The colour is what people come for. Mineral deposits stain the ground and the pools in oranges, greens and yellows that look almost artificial in photographs and are somehow more intense in person. The paths suit most fitness levels and the full circuit takes a couple of hours.

Local tip: The free Mud Pools and Hot 'n' Cold streams sit just up the same road. Worth combining into one afternoon rather than treating this as a standalone stop.

A short 1.7km forest loop near the Redwoods, known for the glow worm dell at Cascade Falls. Free, with no facilities on site.

Two completely different walks depending on when you go. Mossy native bush by day and a glow worm display after dark, on a loop short enough to do both in one evening.

Local tip: Bring a torch but switch it off once you reach the falls. Your eyes need a few minutes in the dark before the glow worms become visible.

A conservation centre for the kārearea, New Zealand's native falcon, with a breeding programme and live flying displays. Paid entry, near the Redwoods area.

The kārearea is rarer than the kiwi and most New Zealanders have never seen one. The flying displays put the birds in the air at close range, which is the only realistic way to appreciate how fast they actually are.

Local tip: Plan your visit around the flying display times rather than just wandering in. That is when the birds perform, not while they are sitting in their enclosures.

A living geothermal village where a Te Arawa community still lives among active mud pools, steam vents and the Pohutu Geyser. Guided tours cover the history of the settlement, traditional cooking using geothermal steam and the surrounding thermal terraces. Paid entry.

This is a working village rather than a reconstruction and that is the whole difference. People here have used the steam and the boiling pools for cooking and bathing for generations and still do. The tours are led by residents so the history comes first hand.

A 5-star motel on Fenton Street with its own day spa and private spa pools available in-room, a genuine step up from standard motel amenities.

Complimentary retro bikes are available to guests so central Rotorua is easy to explore without a car. The in-room pools are the main draw for anyone who wants a soak without heading out to one of the commercial complexes.

A historic pub on Tutanekai Street set inside a former police station. Live bands play Thursday to Saturday.

The bar carries a solid range of Moa beers alongside the usual pub fare. The building does a lot of the work here and the live music makes it one of the better late options at this end of town.

A 4-star motel on Lake Road, part of the Bella Vista chain found across New Zealand. It sits near a dairy and a fish and chip shop.

Convenient rather than distinctive. Useful for a practical stay though without much personality of its own compared to some of Rotorua's individually run motels.

A 4.5-star hotel on the edge of Rotorua's CBD, bordering Government Gardens with Polynesian Spa right next door.

The position makes it one of the most convenient picks if a soak is on the agenda. Eat Streat and the lakefront are both within easy walking distance, so it works as a base for anyone wanting to stay central without needing a car for evenings out.

An upmarket fish and chips takeaway in the tree-lined streets of Sunnybrook, run by owner Isabel, formerly the executive chef at Pullman Rotorua. Small setup with limited seating, mostly takeaway.

The menu puts a Filipino spin on the Kiwi classic. Battered fish is served on pandesal, a slightly sweet Filipino bread roll made locally, alongside adobo fish tacos, smash burgers and kumara fries with chipotle mayo. A long way from a standard chippie.

A steep out and back track to the 757m summit of Mt Ngongotaha, starting from Violet Bonnington Reserve. Native forest and birdlife along the way. Free.

Worth knowing before you commit that there is no view at the top. The climb and the bush are the point, so do not go expecting a summit payoff.

Local tip: The adjoining Nature Loop Track is easier and has a lookout with panoramic views over Rotorua partway up. The summit itself does not.

A campground built right around Te Manaroa Spring, one of the largest natural hot springs in the Southern Hemisphere.

Campers get free unlimited access to the onsite hot pool complex for the whole stay, which makes it better value than the nightly rate suggests. Soak as many times a day as you like.

A 51km cycle trail linking Rotorua's geothermal landmarks, running from Government Gardens out toward Waiotapu and Waikite Valley. Free to ride and rideable in shorter sections.

The full route is a serious day out but the trail was built to be broken up, so most riders take a section rather than committing to the whole thing.

Local tip: The first stretch out to Whakarewarewa Forest is an easy scenic taster if you are short on time.

A privately run wildlife and natural springs park at 467 Paradise Valley Road, about 10 to 15 minutes west of Rotorua. Open every day of the year from 8am until dark, with last entry at 5pm. Free parking on site.

Spring-fed streams and display pools hold hundreds of rainbow and brown trout, viewable at eye level through an underwater window. You can hand feed deer, wallabies, goats, alpacas, donkeys and emus, and walk through the kea aviary to see New Zealand's alpine parrot up close. An elevated treetops walkway runs through the bush canopy in a quieter corner of the park. The freshwater spring is drinkable straight from the source.

The pride of African lions is the outlier here and the reason a lot of people come. It is one of very few lion enclosures in the country and the viewing is close.

Local tip: Lion feeding is at 2.30pm every day, with kea and possum feeding at 3pm. Time your visit around those or the lions will most likely be asleep. Allow one to two hours.

A cafe on Ngongotaha Road, near the lakeside lodges on the western side of Lake Rotorua.

It serves the Ngongotaha area rather than the central CBD cluster, which makes it a useful stop if you are based out this side of the lake rather than in town.

A 1.7km loop past one of the clearest freshwater springs in the country, where the water holds a near-constant temperature year round and the bed is visible many metres down. The path winds through tall redwoods and along the spring-fed stream to Lake Rotorua. Now paid entry after previously being free.

The clarity is the whole appeal. Looking straight down through several metres of water to the sand at the bottom is a strange thing to see and photographs never quite catch it.

Kawerau's main freedom camping spot, centrally located and within walking distance of both the Maurie Kjar hot pools and the i-SITE. Certified self-contained vehicles only, no tents.

Four powered sites are available. A bond plus key fee is payable through the i-SITE. Free for the first three nights, then roughly $10 to $12 a night after that, up to a maximum stay of 7 nights.

Excavated ruins and a museum on the village destroyed by the 1886 Mt Tarawera eruption. Paid entry, and the site includes a bush walk down to a waterfall.

The eruption buried the village in ash overnight and the excavation puts you directly among what was left of it. This is the most tangible account of the 1886 event anywhere in the region.

Local tip: A lot of visitors miss the walk down to Te Wairoa Falls at the end. It is an extra 20 minutes and worth it.

A cafe and eatery on Fenton Street right beside the i-SITE, set in a historic building with a British racing green colour scheme and art deco touches.

House-roasted Okere Falls coffee and a seasonally changing brunch menu with strong vegan options through the day. In the evening it shifts into a craft beer library with cocktails, wine and cider, so it covers both ends of the day rather than shutting at three like most of the cafes nearby.

A small family-run Korean restaurant on Pukuatua Street, consistently rated as Rotorua's best Korean dining.

The menu runs through traditional meats, soups and side dishes alongside a self-cook BBQ buffet, with unlimited refills on rice and banchan. The refills are what make it good value for a group.

A 4WD adventure park with monster truck rides, mud pits and a range of off-road vehicles from Argos to purpose-built trucks. Paid, sitting alongside the Skyline and Velocity Valley cluster.

Professional drivers handle most of the rides though some experiences put you behind the wheel. Being in the passenger seat is not the soft option here. The trucks go places that look impossible from the outside.

A 4-star hotel on Fairy Springs Road, positioned next to Skyline Rotorua and Mitai Māori Village rather than in the central Eat Streat area. A restaurant, bar and coffee shop are all on site, along with a shared lounge and hot springs.

It is also one of the more unusual accommodation setups in Rotorua. Alongside the standard hotel rooms there is a separate budget capsule-room building nearby with shared bathrooms, aimed at solo travellers. Two very different price points on one site.

A Rotorua institution on Tutanekai Street since the early 1980s, sitting at the lake end of Eat Streat. Ranked in TripAdvisor's top 10 ice cream parlours in New Zealand.

Over 40 flavours are on offer but the Danish cone is the signature order. A large waffle cone with up to three flavours, toppings, whipped cream and nuts or sprinkles. Order one and commit, because there is no elegant way to eat it.

A Fijian-Indian fusion takeaway in Selwyn Heights, blending traditional Pacific Island cooking with Kiwi takeaway classics. Family-run with a strong local reputation for friendly service.

The menu runs from butter chicken pies and lamb shank curry through to fried rice, roast meals and a well-regarded fish and chips. Portions are generous and the prices are reasonable, which is most of the reason it has the following it does.

A straightforward vehicle-accessible DOC campsite on the shore of Lake Rerewhakaaitu, suited to cars, campervans and tents alike.

No major standout feature beyond the lake itself. What it does have is easy access, without the boat-or-walk-in restrictions that limit several of the other lakeside sites in the region.

A series of naturally hot pools at varying temperatures, fed by Te Manaroa Spring, one of the largest natural hot springs in the Southern Hemisphere. Paid entry, with an onsite campground.

The range of temperatures is the useful part. You can work your way from a mild pool up to something genuinely hot rather than being stuck with one setting.

Local tip: The spring itself is visible for free on a short walk from the car park, even if you do not pay to use the pools.

A pedestrian-only dining precinct at the lake end of Tutanekai Street. Cuisine ranges from pub fare and steaks to Italian, Indian, Thai and tapas, with live music through busier evenings and a family-friendly atmosphere earlier in the night.

The timber verandahs on each restaurant frontage were deliberately designed to reflect the region's forestry and wood-processing heritage. Closing the street to traffic is what makes it work. You can walk the whole strip and read every menu before committing.

High-speed jet boat tours across Lake Rotorua, with add-on trips to Mokoia Island and the boat-access-only Manupirua Hot Springs on the far shore. Also runs parasailing. Paid, departing from the lakefront.

The Manupirua add-on is the one worth knowing about. Those springs cannot be reached by road at all, so a boat trip is the only way in.

A free 3.7km return walk to a public viewpoint looking directly across at Pohutu Geyser and the wider Whakarewarewa thermal valley, without paying for entry to Te Puia. The track winds through bush and open ground on the opposite side of the valley.

The view is genuine if slightly more distant, taking in the geyser in full eruption along with the surrounding steam and mineral terraces. A good option on a tighter budget, or for locals who have already done the paid experience and just want to check the geyser is still putting on a show.

Local tip: Pohutu erupts most reliably in the morning, so this is worth timing rather than wandering up whenever suits.

An award-winning evening Māori cultural experience, formerly known as Tamaki Māori Village, with haka, storytelling and a hangi dinner in a recreated village setting deep in native forest. Paid, and usually includes bus transport from Rotorua.

The forest setting is what sets it apart from the venue-based options. Transport is generally part of the package so there is no need to sort a driver for the evening.

A free, always open thermal park covering around 12 hectares right on the edge of Rotorua's CBD, built around a large steaming lake formed by geothermal activity.

Walking paths circle the lake past bubbling mud pools, fenced-off boiling pools and vents releasing steam straight out of the ground, all just metres from the footpath. It is one of the few places in Rotorua where you get this close to raw geothermal activity without paying for entry. There is also a playground, open lawns and a Saturday market.

An adults-only luxury hot springs and day spa on the Rotorua lakefront near Sulphur Point, with tiered mineral pools cascading down toward the water. Treatments and wellness packages are available alongside general pool entry. Paid entry.

The adults-only policy is the point of difference from the family complexes elsewhere in town. Quieter, and set up for a long soak rather than a swim.

Local tip: Late afternoon sessions catch the sunset over the lake from the pools.

A DOC campsite on Millar Road, about 15 minutes from Rotorua, suiting tents, cars and motorhomes alike. That combination is rarer than it sounds given most of the region's lakeside sites restrict you to one or the other.

The lake offers swimming, kayaking and fishing straight from the campsite, which makes it a genuine base rather than just somewhere to park up and sleep.

An award-winning pie bakery on Old Taupo Road, founded by Patrick Lam and holder of more than 70 baking awards including multiple NZ Bakels Supreme Pie Awards.

Alongside the classics like mince and cheese, the bakery is known for pushing into unusual territory. Roast duck, lamb, even rum, pineapple and coconut. Sandwiches, cakes and hot food like chicken kebabs and hotdogs round out the counter. Outdoor seating and a window to watch the bakers at work.

A Japanese restaurant on Pukuatua Street with dedicated sushi bar seating.

Straightforward and solid rather than adventurous. A reliable option for Japanese food in central Rotorua when you want something lighter than the Eat Streat lineup.

The world's youngest geothermal system, created by the 1886 Tarawera eruption. A gentle downhill walk of one to two hours passes Frying Pan Lake and the pastel coloured Inferno Crater Lake, with an optional boat cruise on Lake Rotomahana at the end. Paid entry.

Everything here has formed since 1886, which makes it geologically brand new. The walk runs downhill the whole way so it is easier than the distance suggests, and there is a shuttle back up from the bottom.

A zipline and canopy tour through native forest west of Ngongotaha, tied to an active predator free conservation programme. Paid, with check in and shuttle from a separate office on Fairy Springs Road.

The conservation angle is not window dressing. The forest is under active pest control and the guides work the ecology into the tour, so it lands as more than just a ride through the trees.

Local tip: Check in happens at the Fairy Springs Road office, not at the forest. Do not drive straight to the site.

A Mexican restaurant on Tutanekai Street, right on Eat Streat, established in 2017 by Eduardo Diaz and Cristina Allen. The menu is built around parrillada and ceviche with a full range of cocktails, Mexican beers and Jarritos.

Regulars rate it as some of the best Mexican food outside Mexico. Free salsa lessons run on Tuesdays and there is live music on weekends, which gives it a livelier atmosphere than the other restaurants on the strip.

A natural hot pool on the shore of Lake Tarawera, where you dig your own warm soak in the sand at the water's edge with the cool lake right beside it. Free to use.

It sits at the end of the Tarawera Trail so it is the reward waiting at the far end of that walk, though it is also reachable directly by boat or water taxi if you would rather skip the track. Switching between the hot sand pool and the cold lake is the whole experience.

Local tip: There is a basic DOC campground right here too if you want to stay overnight rather than just visiting for the day. A hot pool and a campsite in one spot is a rare combination.

A tapas and wine bar with an entrance that is easy to walk straight past, tucked away rather than fronting onto the street.

A quieter and more intimate option for shared plates and wine compared to the louder Eat Streat venues. Worth seeking out if you want a conversation rather than a soundtrack.

A remote undeveloped natural hot pool near Waiotapu, formed where a spout of geothermal water pours down into a swimming hole deep enough to sit in with water at chest height. Bush on all sides. Reached by a short walk in from a roadside car park off The Avenue, about 500m along.

Visitors have long rated it one of the most beautiful and least crowded of the free thermal soaks in the area. There are no facilities at all, so bring everything you need.

Local tip: Avoid submerging your head in untreated thermal water anywhere in this area. There is a small but real health risk from certain freshwater organisms.

A 3km return walk past three waterfalls on the Kaituna River, with views of rafters and kayakers running the rapids below. Free.

The rafting is half the entertainment. You get an overhead view of commercial trips dropping through the falls, which is a better vantage point than the rafters themselves get.

Local tip: There is a good swimming hole partway along if you are visiting on a hot day.

A working kiwi breeding and incubation facility inside Rainbow Springs Nature Park, contributing chicks back to wild populations as part of a national conservation effort.

Guided tours let you see eggs being candled and chicks being hand raised behind glass. This is an operating hatchery rather than a display, so what you see depends on what stage the current birds are at.

A 3-star motel on Whakaue Street, just steps from Eat Streat and one of the most central locations available despite the lower star rating.

Free bikes and scooters are available to guests along with access to thermal pools. A solid value pick for anyone prioritising location and freebies over five-star polish.

Formal English style gardens on the shore of Lake Rotorua, surrounding the earthquake damaged Rotorua Museum. Bowling green, rose beds and statuary throughout.

The contrast is the appeal. Manicured Edwardian gardens sitting on ground that still steams in places, with the lake on one side and the thermal areas on the other.

A geothermal reserve and spa 15 minutes northeast of Rotorua, owned by local iwi Ngāti Rangiteaorere and built around the therapeutic use of mud and sulphur water that has been part of Māori healing practice here for centuries.

The on-site Wai Ora Spa is the main draw. Full-body mud baths, sulphur spa pools and combination packages that put you through both, with most treatments running 60 to 90 minutes. Private pools and more secluded options are available for anyone who would rather not share with other visitors.

The mud and mineral water are drawn straight from the reserve itself, which makes it a genuinely different experience from a standard day spa. More raw and earthy than polished.

A holiday park in Koutu with its own geothermal pool and an onsite hangi pit.

That pairing ties the accommodation to an actual traditional Māori cooking experience rather than just being somewhere to sleep. The geothermal setting runs through the whole park rather than being a single feature bolted on the side.

Kawerau's free geothermally heated public pools, right in the town centre opposite the i-SITE. No entry fee.

The complex includes a large pool split into a 25m and 5m section, a spa pool, kids' pools and a newer water park. Free geothermal swimming at this scale is rare anywhere in the country.

A quiet 2km loop through native forest with glimpses of two small lakes, Rotongata and Rotoatu.

Less visited than the bigger-name walks in the region and the birdwatching is better for it. A good choice if the Redwoods tracks feel too busy.

One of New Zealand's best known mountain bike networks, with over 100km of trails through redwood and native forest for all skill levels. Free trail access, bike hire extra.

The range is what makes it work for everyone. Gentle forest doubletrack through to serious downhill runs, all off the same network, so mixed-ability groups can ride the same day without splitting up.

Local tip: Hire bikes at the forest entrance itself rather than in town. It saves an unpleasant ride on roads just to reach the trailhead.

A farm show built around sheep, featuring shearing demonstrations, multiple breeds on display, working dog trials and lamb feeding.

It is aimed squarely at visitors who have never been on a working farm and it does that job well. The dog trials tend to be the part people remember.

A modern licensed cafe on Arawa Street run by Chanchal and Varun, blending Indian culinary influences with local Kiwi tastes. Everything is made from scratch in small batches with a seasonally changing menu.

Standout dishes include the warm winter porridge with sweet spice and homemade granola, alongside eggs benedict and kumara chips that get singled out in reviews. The Indian influence sits underneath the menu rather than dominating it.

A set of free communal geothermal foot-soaking pools tucked into one corner of Kuirau Park, near the playground. No entry fee and no booking. Just turn up and find a spot on the edge.

The water comes from the same thermal system as the rest of the park, kept at a soakable temperature rather than the boiling point of the pools nearby. It is a popular stop for locals as well as visitors passing through, which tells you most of what you need to know.

Local tip: Bring your own towel. It can get busy.

An evening Māori cultural experience with a haka performance, hangi dinner and a glow worm stream walk on site.

Having the glow worms on the same grounds is what separates it from the other evening experiences. You get two things in one visit without driving anywhere else.

Local tip: Arrive early enough to do the glow worm walk before the main show starts. It is included but easy to miss if you cut your arrival close.

A two hour guided treetop adventure in the Redwoods, 25 metres above the forest floor on a 650 metre suspended loop. Twenty five jungle themed bridges, three ziplines and an optional treetop leap at the end, all on a continuous belay system with a guide the whole way. Bookings are essential.

This is a separate experience from the self-guided Redwoods Treewalk and it sits 7 metres higher. Guides work in the history of the forest, the native birdlife and Māori legend as you go, so it lands as more than just a ropes course. Entry to the Redwoods Glowworms eco-cave is included in the ticket.

Local tip: Check in at the Altitude hangar in the far corner of the main car park, not at the Treewalk. Arrive 15 minutes before your booked time and allow up to two and a half hours for the whole thing.

Four ziplines flying over the Kaituna River and Tutea Falls at Okere Falls, run jointly by Rotorua Rafting and Ngāti Pikiao. Paid, with onsite parking.

Flying over an active river and a commercially rafted waterfall gives it a different feel to a forest zipline. You are looking down at rafts dropping through the falls while you cross.

Local tip: Often sold as a combo with Kaituna rafting since the same operator runs both at the same spot.

A free freedom camping area near Okere Falls with toilets on site. Certified self-contained vehicles only, no tents.

Free sites with facilities are not common, which makes this one fill up.

Local tip: The location puts you close to the Okere Falls Track, Rotorua Ziplines and the Kaituna rafting operators. A good base if that side of the region is your focus rather than central Rotorua.

Eight natural mineral hot pools on the shore of Lake Rotoiti at Manupirua Bay, each fed by a spring and each running at a different temperature. Reachable only by boat, kayak or floatplane. Open 365 days a year.

The access restriction is the whole reason this place stays as good as it is. No road means no crowds and no development, just pools stepped down the lakeside with clear water directly below them. Soak until you overheat, then dive off the jetty or take the slide into the lake and start again.

Changing rooms and a licensed café are on site, and picnics are welcome with outdoor seating and BBQs available. Moor your own boat at the jetties, take the water taxi, or arrive with one of the tour operators running trips across the lake.

Local tip: Winter is arguably better than summer here. Steam comes off the lake on a cold day and the contrast between the pools and the water is sharper.

A major geothermal reserve and home to the New Zealand Māori Arts and Crafts Institute, where you can watch carvers and weavers training in traditional techniques.

The Pohutu Geyser erupts here multiple times a day and is visible from within the grounds. The carving school is the part that surprises people. These are apprentices working on real commissions rather than a demonstration put on for visitors.

A mini golf course, one of a handful of easy family-friendly options in Rotorua.

Good for filling a spare hour or a rainy afternoon when the outdoor plans fall over.

An authentic Northern Chinese restaurant specialising in handmade dumplings with a wide range of fillings, alongside pork buns and traditional noodle dishes.

Prices are consistently described as wallet-friendly and the dumplings in particular draw comparisons to home cooking from reviewers with a Northern Chinese background. That is about the highest compliment a dumpling house can get.

A licensed café right at the Waipa Mountain Bike Park carpark, on the fringe of the Whakarewarewa Forest and connected to the Mountain Bike Rotorua shop next door. Family-owned. Dog-friendly outdoors with water bowls provided.

The menu is built around gourmet burgers, with the Wagyu beef Trail Burger as the signature order, plus wood-fired pizzas, toasties and a full breakfast and lunch menu. Coffee is barista made from their own house Jungle Coffee beans.

There is indoor seating and a large covered deck looking out over the forest. It is genuinely set up for riders. You can roll straight off the trails onto the front deck for a coffee and a burger.

Private wood-fired outdoor hot tub sessions set in native bush, booked for individual groups rather than shared with other visitors.

A quieter and more secluded alternative to the commercial hot springs parks. Worth it if the appeal of a soak is the peace rather than the facilities.

A café inside Scion's Innovation Centre, Te Whare Nui o Tuteata, on the edge of the Redwoods forest.

The striking timber building reflects Scion's forestry research focus, with exposed beams and a light airy design that draws as much comment from visitors as the food does. Worth going in even if you are not eating.

The menu runs to wood-fired pizzas including a Caprese and a meat-heavy Notorious P.I.G., alongside brunch dishes like a seasonal Green Bowl with halloumi and Turkish Eggs, plus coffee from Atomic Coffee Roasters.

Roll downhill inside a giant inflatable ball, either dry or with water added for a wetter and faster ride.

Rotorua is considered the birthplace of zorbing and this is one of the original operators. The wet version is the one most people pick and it is genuinely quicker than it looks from the top.

An Irish pub on Tutanekai Street serving classic Irish pub food alongside Guinness on tap.

Live music runs on Thursdays with a quiz night on Sundays, which makes it a quieter midweek option than the rest of the strip.

A free freedom camping spot right on the shore of Lake Rotorua, on Hamurana Road. Certified self-contained vehicles only.

Waking up on the lake edge for nothing is the appeal. There are no facilities so you need to be genuinely self-contained rather than technically compliant.

A cafe, store and craft beer garden combined, out at Okere Falls opposite Lake Rotoiti and right next door to Rotorua Ziplines.

House-roasted coffee using the same beans as Mr Wolf, award-winning toasties, and a genuinely eco-focused operation. Biodegradable everything, a vegetable garden out back and a stock of organic and artisan groceries alongside the cafe menu.

The beer garden is the reason most people stay longer than they planned. An easy stop if you are already out this way for the falls or the rafting.

A gondola up Mt Ngongotaha with a luge track, zipline and Sky Swing at the top, plus mountain biking trails and a restaurant with panoramic views over the lake.

The luge is the main event and it is the reason people buy multiple rides rather than one. Everything sits at the top of the gondola so one trip up covers the lot.

A flat 5.2km return lakeside walk through wetlands at Lake Ōkāreka, popular with locals for an easy morning walk.

Flat the whole way and well formed, which makes it one of the more accessible walks in the region. The lake is also used for swimming and kayaking if you want to make more of it.

A long established mineral pool complex on the Rotorua lakefront, drawing on two different natural springs, one acidic and one alkaline, each said to have different therapeutic properties. Separate adult-only and family pool areas.

Having two spring sources is unusual and it means the pools genuinely differ from each other rather than just varying in temperature. The split between adult-only and family areas keeps both crowds happy.

Free to view bubbling grey mud pools just off the Waiotapu Loop Road, with a boardwalk viewing platform.

The mud plops and bursts constantly so there is always something happening. The sulphur smell is strong and unavoidable. Ten minutes here is usually enough and it costs nothing.

A Rotorua institution on Arawa Street, open since 1995 and serving from 7am. Big breakfasts, brunch, lunch and cabinet treats through the day, with a bar attached for later.

The room is the first thing people mention. Quirky fit-out, paw prints running through it and hand-painted table numbers, all a long way from the polished cafe look. Servings are generous and built on fresh local produce. The corned beef hash comes up in review after review, and the Woofer is the order for anyone who intends to skip lunch afterwards.

The menu covers a lot of ground, with a strong vegetarian and vegan section, a kids menu and freshly squeezed juices alongside the coffee. It works for a family breakfast, a solo flat white or a long lunch equally well.

Local tip: It fills up fast at weekend breakfast. Service moves quicker than the queue suggests, so do not walk away if it looks full.

The original Kaituna rafting company, operating since 1991. Founded by long time raft guide and kayaker Keith Hughes, who ran the river with anyone willing to come along back when it was considered unraftable, opening it up to commercial rafting in the first place.

Based at 18 Okere Falls Road, the trip tackles the Kaituna's Grade 5 section. Fourteen rapids through native rainforest, including the 7 metre Tutea Falls, the highest commercially rafted waterfall in the world. The base sits directly on the riverbank so there is no long shuttle ride and no waiting around in a wetsuit.

Run today by Pete Lodge and Julian "Blue" Mathison, both former guides who took over from Hughes after 26 years. It is consistently rated the top rafting company in Rotorua on Tripadvisor, with more than three decades on this exact stretch of river behind it.

Local tip: The Okere Falls Track starts nearby and gives you an overhead view of the rapids you are about to run. Worth doing before rather than after.

A historic thermal village on the shore of Lake Rotorua, still home to a living Māori community.

St Faith's Anglican Church here is known for its etched glass window of Christ, positioned so he appears to be walking on the surface of the lake behind it. This is a residential village rather than an attraction, so visit with that in mind.

A dramatic waterfall where the Tarawera River bursts straight out of the cliff face after flowing underground for part of its course.

Access requires a forestry permit from the Kawerau i-SITE, available on weekends and public holidays. The water emerging from solid rock rather than flowing over the top of it is genuinely unusual and worth the permit hassle.

Local tip: Buy the permit in Kawerau before you drive out. There is nowhere to get one at the falls themselves.

A 2.1km loop through old growth forest within the Mokaihaha Ecological Area, with dense canopy cover for most of the walk.

Old growth is the draw. The canopy closes over the track almost entirely, which makes it feel much more remote than the distance suggests.

Local tip: It gets muddy and slippery after rain. Wear something with grip.

A free natural hot pool that runs consistently very hot, with a small waterfall feeding into the main pool. No facilities on site. Bring a towel and expect an unmarked roadside car park that fills up on weekends.

The waterfall is the feature. Sitting under falling hot water in the middle of bush costs nothing and is the reason this one is so well known.

Local tip: Avoid submerging your head in any natural thermal water in this area, including here. There is a small but real health risk from certain freshwater organisms in untreated volcanic water.

A 4.5-star hotel built around old-world elegance, one of Rotorua's more character-filled stays rather than a standard modern hotel.

High Tea is served on site alongside an onsite cabaret and a private thermal pool. That gives it a genuinely different flavour to the CBD hotel cluster. More heritage charm than convenience-driven amenities.

A 3.4km loop through the Memorial Grove redwoods and tree ferns, passing a small distinctly blue spring partway around.

The redwoods and the tree ferns growing under them make for an odd mix of Californian and New Zealand forest in the same frame. The spring is small and easy to walk past if you are not looking for it.

A free thermal soak where a hot stream and a cold stream meet near Waiotapu Bridge, letting you find your own comfortable temperature. No facilities and no car park.

Being able to adjust the heat by moving a metre or two is what makes this one different from the fixed-temperature pools nearby.

Local tip: Locals often rate this over Kerosene Creek precisely because you can move toward the hot or cold side to set the temperature yourself.

A 15 to 16km one-way track following the western and southern shores of Lake Tarawera, starting at the Te Wairoa car park just past Blue Lake on Tarawera Road. Free to walk, though the water taxi and campsite both carry separate fees.

The path stays mostly in native bush close to the water, climbing over a few headlands that open onto broad views across the lake, with the bulk of Mt Tarawera visible for much of the walk. Around the 7km mark there is a steep climb up to Rotomahana Lookout, looking down over both Lake Tarawera and Lake Rotomahana at once.

The track then descends over the final stretch to Te Rātā Bay and Hot Water Beach, where natural geothermal springs let you dig your own warm pool right at the lake's edge. Most people take 4 to 6 hours one way and return by pre-booked water taxi rather than walking back out.

Local tip: Book the water taxi well ahead, especially over summer. It only runs on demand and it is a long way back if you have assumed you can just turn up.

A cluster of adventure rides on a purpose-built circuit, including Freefall Xtreme indoor skydiving, the Swoop swing ride, Rotorua Bungy and the Agrojet jet boat thrill ride. Pay per activity or as a combo.

Having four separate rides on one site is the appeal. You can spend a full morning here without moving the car, and the combo pricing makes doing several cheaper than picking one.

A historic Māori portage track between Lake Rotoiti and Lake Rotoehu, passing a sacred matai tree known as the Wishing Tree, where a well-known ancestress is said to have met her husband.

Portage tracks were how waka moved between lakes and this one has been in use for centuries. The history is the reason to walk it rather than the scenery.

Local tip: There are swimming and picnic spots at Korokitewao Bay on the Rotoiti end if you want to make a longer stop of it.

A buffet restaurant at the top of Mt Ngongotaha, reached via the Skyline Gondola, with panoramic views over Lake Rotorua and the city below.

A scenic choice as much as a dining one. Popular for groups and special occasions given the setting, and the gondola ride up is part of the evening rather than just transport.

Officially Maunga Kākaramea, meaning multi-coloured mountain, named for its mineral-stained slopes.

A summit track climbs to a lookout, with a shorter option to a crater lake viewpoint for anyone with less time. The colours on the slopes are the reason for the name and they are best in clear light.

An easy walking track around Lake Tikitapu, one of the most photographed lakes in the Rotorua district thanks to its striking almost artificial-looking blue colour. The colour comes from fine white pumice and rhyolite on the lake bed reflecting light back up through the clear water. Free.

The circuit is flat, well formed and shaded by native bush for most of its length, so it suits most fitness levels. There are regular access points down to the lake for a swim on the way round.

Part of the track also passes a glow worm dell, so the same walk that is a pleasant daytime stroll becomes a completely different experience after dark. It sits right next to Blue Lake Top 10 Holiday Park if you want to make a longer stop of it.

Local tip: Go around dusk to catch both the last of the daylight swimming and the glow worms coming out, rather than committing to one or the other.

A freedom camping spot with 17 spaces right in Government Gardens, in the heart of central Rotorua. No facilities on site and certified self-contained vehicles only.

The central location is the whole draw. Walking distance to the lakefront, Eat Streat and Polynesian Spa, which is unheard of for a free site.

Local tip: That central position also makes it one of the most sought-after spots in town. Arrive reasonably early to secure a space.

A geothermal walking and biking area along the Rotorua lakefront, with steaming vents right beside the path and boardwalks over the hottest ground.

It is also part of a wildlife refuge for waterfowl, so you get birdlife and active geothermal ground on the same flat easy route straight out of town.

Scenic floatplane and helicopter flights over Mt Tarawera and out toward White Island, departing from the lakefront.

Some helicopter options include a landing on Tarawera's crater rim, which is the only way to stand on it. The 1886 eruption scar reads completely differently from the air than it does from the ground.
